slides.page_title: Causal Consistency: Read Your Own Writes

blocks.title: Cluster Time
items: Nodes gossip `$clusterTime` on every message
It is signed, so a client cannot forge a future time
That signature is why you cannot skip replication waits

blocks.title: Cheaper than a transaction
blocks.text: Transactions are causally consistent by construction. If you only need ordering and not atomicity, a causal session costs far less — just some read latency waiting for replication.

items: Since 4.2 one transaction can touch multiple shards
`mongos` coordinates the whole thing for the client
A single-shard txn skips coordination entirely
One participating shard is elected transaction coordinator
Prepared shards write a prepare oplog entry
The decision is durable in `config.transaction_coordinators`
Only then does each shard actually commit

blocks.title: Shard key is the lever
blocks.text: Co-locate documents that must change together — same shard key prefix — and the transaction stays single-shard. That is the whole performance story.

items: readConcern must be snapshot, or majority/local
`snapshot` uses a global cluster-wide timestamp
`readPreference` secondary is not allowed
A shard cannot join the transaction once commit begins
A chunk migration conflicting with an in-flight txn aborts it
In-progress prepared txns block chunk migration
They also block some DDL until they resolve

blocks.title: Killed mongos
blocks.text: The coordinator finishes the job without it. The client gets UnknownTransactionCommitResult and must retry commitTransaction — not the whole transaction.

lines: // watch these before blaming the network

blocks.title: Design Checklist
items: Keep the txn on one shard where you can
Never span shards for a bulk job
Measure participating shard count, not just latency
Transient covers write conflict, stepdown, NoSuchTransaction
It means nothing applied — safe to run from the beginning
Unknown-commit means the commit may or may not have landed

blocks.title: Let the driver do it
blocks.text: `withTransaction` implements both loops correctly. Hand-rolled retries almost always get the commit-unknown case wrong.

items: A periodic cleanup thread kills transactions past the lifetime
You get `Transaction with { txnNumber } has been aborted`
The fix is a smaller transaction, not a bigger limit
Pre-4.2 the total writes had to fit one 16 MB oplog entry
4.2+ splits the transaction into multiple oplog entries
The 16 MB cap on an individual document still stands
Automatic abort on primary stepdown or election
Automatic abort when the session is reaped
Manual: `killSessions`, or `killOp` on the txn's opid

blocks.title: Keep The Snapshot Young
items: No network calls between start and commit
No user input, no long computation
The snapshot ages the entire time you wait

blocks.title: Idempotency detail
blocks.text: Because the callback re-runs, generate ObjectIds OUTSIDE it. Otherwise a retry writes a different `_id` than the attempt you thought failed.

items: Model to avoid them — embed, or accept eventual consistency
Keep them short — under 1000 docs, well under 60 seconds
Keep them narrow — fewer collections, fewer shards, fewer conflicts

blocks.title: Index the filters
blocks.text: Index every field the transaction filters on. A collection scan inside a transaction holds the snapshot open far longer than the work deserves.

items: A version field plus a filter — no snapshot held open
Zero `modifiedCount` means someone else won the race
Cheapest fix when only one document has to change
State change and its event land in one write scope
A worker republishes until the consumer acknowledges
Delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers stay idempotent

blocks.title: Avoid the hot document
blocks.text: One global stats document updated by every order serializes the whole system. Shard the counter across buckets, or aggregate it offline.

items: Missing `{ session }` on one op — it commits and never rolls back
Hand-rolled retry replaying a commit-unknown error twice
Implicit collection creation inside a txn on pre-4.4 servers
Skipping `endSession`, exhausting the server session pool
Assuming serializability — it is snapshot, so write skew bites
`count()` inside a txn errors — use `countDocuments()`
`readPreference` secondary is rejected inside a transaction
Write concern set per-operation inside a txn is an error

blocks.title: Read the label, not the message
blocks.text: Branch on the error label before anything else. It alone tells you whether to replay the whole transaction or only retry the commit.

blocks.q: What does a transaction actually cost?
a_bullets: Single-shard: about a normal write plus one commit round-trip
Multi-shard: that, multiplied by prepare and decide phases
Contention cost dwarfs both once a hot document appears

items: If most operations need a txn, the schema is relational-shaped
Embedding related data makes atomicity free
Document-level atomicity already covers roughly 90% of cases

blocks.title: Closing Checklist
items: Session passed to every single operation
`withTransaction` used, callback idempotent
readConcern and writeConcern chosen deliberately
Transaction short, narrow, hot documents avoided

caption.text: Part 2 of MONGODB TRANSACTIONS. MongoDB gives you atomicity for free inside one document — the moment you need two, you inherit sessions, snapshots, write conflicts and a two-phase commit. This handbook is the whole path: the core API, read and write concern, why snapshot isolation still lets write skew through, what changes on a sharded cluster, and the two error labels that decide whether you retry the transaction or just the commit. Save it for the day a transfer has to land on both sides.
